Aug 2026 stability assessment

IIT Mandi + partners5

Researchers Dhiman, Singh, Shukla, KC & Gupta combined geotechnical modelling, field work and high-resolution satellite observation. They used the Limit Equilibrium Method to estimate Factor of Safety, and the Finite Element Method to estimate Strength Reduction Factor.5

Core mechanism: rainfall and groundwater infiltration raise pore-water pressure inside the fractured slope, which lowers its effective shear strength — the primary driver behind renewed movement.5

Where the concern is concentrated

Profile 4Lowest Factor of Safety in the study — the most unstable section modelled.High
Right flankContinued tension cracking — flagged as a priority for monitoring & mitigation.High
Profiles 2 & 3Also found vulnerable; joint sets broadly follow the slope angle, a favourable failure plane.Elevated
Upper crownTension cracks first appeared here, defining the upper boundary of the slide mass.Watch

Concern levels are the study's qualitative ranking, not numeric Factor-of-Safety values — the source article doesn't publish exact FoS figures, so none are invented here.5

Recommended by the study

  • Intensified, year-round monitoring of the slope
  • Controlled surface & sub-surface drainage
  • Suitable retaining structures on the right flank
  • Geotextile reinforcement beneath soil cover
  • Strengthened vegetation cover
  • Early-warning instrumentation, prioritised at the most vulnerable profiles

The researchers also called for detailed in-situ joint/lithology surveys and full 3D FEM modelling — and noted that earthquakes, rainfall intensity and external loading remain hard to simulate precisely.5

Recurrence timeline

ISPRS 20202
13 Aug 1977

First recorded major failure at this scarp.

13 Aug 1997

Reactivation — visible on early-2000s satellite imagery.

13 Aug 2007

Minor reactivation; limited attention at the time.

12–13 Aug 2017

Catastrophic failure — 46–48 dead, NH‑154 buried, two buses swept ≈800 m downslope.1

All four events cluster around mid-August — the historical peak of the SW monsoon here.

What's live vs. sourced vs. historical

Live — fetched from Open‑Meteo when this page loads; refreshes on demand.
Regional, current — from today's news reporting, dated.
Published research — peer‑reviewed or institutional studies, dated and cited.
Historical record — the documented 2017 disaster and its precursors.
Simulated — the Satellite tab's DEM/InSAR-style maps, generated from the project's demo dataset, clearly labelled and never presented as a live feed.
Honest scope note. This is a concept monitoring dashboard for a real, well-documented landslide site — it is not connected to a deployed sensor network at Kotrupi itself. No public record confirms a live soil-moisture probe or tiltmeter installed at this exact scarp (instrumentation is exactly what the Aug 2026 study recommends adding). Every figure here is either fetched live from public weather data for these coordinates, or drawn from the cited research and news reporting, with a date. Nothing is invented or estimated to fill a gap.
